title: Completion of full surgical procedures on living patients

concept.text: The innovation is a robotic system that completes an entire surgical procedure on a living patient, controlling the instruments and sequencing the operative steps while a surgeon supervises and can stop it. For a minimally invasive operation, this includes the procedure’s irreversible actions, such as cutting tissue, and the decisions needed to continue safely as anatomy, visibility and tissue behavior change. Any human assistance, including instrument changes, must be explicitly accounted for.

The central distinction is between autonomous execution of selected tasks or a surgical phase and autonomy across a whole operation in living tissue. The supplied SRT-H research demonstrates clipping and cutting in excised tissue, an important enabling capability. Extending that work to a complete operation requires handling omitted steps and the additional demands of a living surgical site, including bleeding and physiological motion.

significance.text: Reliable whole-procedure autonomy would transfer instrument execution and operative sequencing for a demonstrated operation from the surgeon to a supervised robotic system. Teleoperation leaves instrument control with the surgeon; this innovation would change the surgeon’s role during that procedure toward supervision and intervention when necessary. That would be a substantial change in how surgical skill is delivered, even if the system remained restricted to one operation and a defined patient population.

Greater clinical capacity, more consistent execution, lower costs and wider access are plausible downstream benefits, rather than automatic consequences of a successful operation. They depend on complication rates, repeatability, total procedure time, staffing, supervision requirements and the frequency of human rescue. A robot that completes a procedure but requires intensive supervision or frequent interruption might establish an important technical capability without increasing clinical throughput.

The SRT-H preprint describes autonomous radiosurgery and vein access as predecessors operating in comparatively controlled settings. Its account emphasizes the remaining gap to dynamic soft-tissue surgery. Living tissue deforms, moves and can bleed; irreversible actions change the scene in which subsequent decisions must be made. These distinctions explain why success in a structured intervention does not establish whole-procedure surgical competence. The predecessor descriptions come from SRT-H’s discussion and were not independently validated in the supplied review.

The impact would initially apply to the operations and conditions actually demonstrated. Competence in other procedures, or operation without an available surgeon, would require additional evidence and capabilities. Everyday robot generality does not itself establish safe manipulation of living tissue, where errors may be irreversible and the episode cannot simply be reset. General verification methods could contribute to safety assurance, but their usefulness for certification is a separate proposition from demonstrating autonomous surgery.

missing_breakthrough.text: The target capability is reliable procedure-level autonomy under the conditions of living surgery. The supplied May 2025 SRT-H preprint identifies changing surgical scenes, anatomical variation, tissue dynamics, bleeding and motion as challenges. Its ex vivo experiments address part of anatomical variation and include actual cuts, but do not demonstrate completion of an operation under these combined physiological demands. The supplied evidence does not establish whether the target remains unmet across the field as of November 1, 2026.

A whole operation requires more than repeating a successful motion on a recognized structure. The robot must identify relevant anatomy, maintain an actionable understanding as tissue is exposed or altered, and select safe subsequent actions. SRT-H explicitly identifies a lack of clinical and anatomical knowledge and places breathing motion beyond the complexity demonstrated. It also acknowledges vulnerability to conditions outside the model’s experience. Those limitations matter because unfamiliar anatomy or a changing view can affect the safety of the next irreversible action.

The engineering gap also includes operating within the actual surgical site and integrating the equipment needed for the entire procedure. The preprint identifies fitting wrist cameras through laparoscopic ports as an in-vivo deployment challenge. Its experiments required manual clip loading and instrument changes. Completing a whole procedure therefore requires either incorporating those functions into the autonomous system or defining and measuring them as assistance, alongside reliable handling of interruptions and equipment problems.

As an engineering synthesis, a convincing system would also need to recognize when continued autonomous action is unsafe, pause appropriately and support timely surgeon takeover. The missing advance is the integration of perception, clinical reasoning, manipulation and recovery across the full procedure. Progress in any one component would be valuable but would not by itself establish that integrated capability.

current_state.text: In the May 15, 2025 SRT-H preprint, Ji Woong Kim and colleagues report successful autonomous execution of the clipping-and-cutting phase across eight unseen ex vivo porcine gallbladders: eight successes in eight experiments, reported as 100%. The phase comprised 17 tasks, and the authors describe the achievement as step-level autonomy. This is a result for a selected phase on excised tissue, rather than a complete cholecystectomy or an operation on a living patient.

The experimental setup limits the breadth of that result. Tissue was manually dissected beforehand, leaving substantial operative work outside the autonomous demonstration. Approximately 10% of gallbladders were excluded because of anatomical anomalies. Successful performance across the selected unseen specimens therefore demonstrates some adaptation to anatomical variation, while leaving performance on excluded anatomies and the full operative sequence unresolved.

The reported absence of human intervention applies to autonomous task execution within that phase. Operators reloaded clips, changed instruments and resumed execution between tasks; the reported duration excludes clip loading and operator-performed tool changes. The paper also reports a scissors replacement and three robot reinitializations during manual tool changes. These details qualify the operational meaning of autonomy without negating the reported success of the automated clipping and cutting.

The authors identify operation in the surgical site, bleeding, tissue motion and unfamiliar conditions as remaining challenges. Their discussion places breathing motion and the clinical and anatomical knowledge needed for more advanced autonomy beyond the demonstrated level. Moving from this ex vivo phase to in-vivo studies, and eventually human studies, is a research direction described in the supplied material, not an achieved result.

The supplied research gives a Science Robotics publication citation dated July 9, 2025, with DOI 10.1126/scirobotics.adt5254. However, the source index contains no retained journal-page material, so the supplied review could not verify the journal abstract or the attributed author response describing work in pig cadavers. The narrower description supported by the retained preprint is ex vivo porcine gallbladder experimentation. Missing journal-page evidence does not establish that the publication details or attributed response are false.

The supplied review relied on a retained, complete, untruncated HTML text of the preprint, with no extraction issues recorded. It did not inspect figures or videos, so the experimental findings here remain author-reported results assessed through that text. No freshness search record was supplied. Consequently, this record establishes a dated 2025 advance and its documented limitations, rather than a comprehensive account of surgical autonomy through November 1, 2026.

completion_criteria.text: A proposed demonstration sequence is completion of a defined minimally invasive procedure in living animals, followed by appropriately evaluated human procedures. The procedure’s boundaries should be specified in advance and include its required irreversible steps. A surgeon may supervise and stop the system, but should not teleoperate the instruments during cases counted as autonomous completions. This animal-to-human sequence is a proposed evaluation approach, not an established completion standard supplied by the sources.
completion_criteria.label: Predefined minimally invasive procedure completed autonomously in living animals then humans

completion_criteria.text: Assistance should be recorded across the entire operative episode. Tool changes and clip loading must either be performed within the autonomous system or explicitly counted as assistance; preparatory dissection, manual resumption, equipment replacement, reinitialization and rescue should also be disclosed. Total procedure time should include these activities. These proposed accounting rules address the specific setup and servicing limits documented in SRT-H, whose automated phase alone would not satisfy the whole-procedure proposal.
completion_criteria.label: Whole-episode assistance and servicing included in total procedure time

completion_criteria.text: A proposed clinical protocol should preregister the primary endpoint, safety thresholds, sample size, eligible anatomy, exclusions, permitted assistance and criteria for stopping or surgeon takeover. It should measure clinically meaningful completion and adverse outcomes, rather than relying only on successful execution of an instrument sequence. No numerical pass threshold or sample size is established by the supplied evidence; those choices remain to be justified for the particular operation and population.
completion_criteria.label: Preregistered protocol measuring clinically meaningful completion and adverse outcomes

completion_criteria.text: One successful case would establish feasibility within that case’s conditions. Stronger evidence would require repeated performance across specified anatomical variation, transparent reporting of failures and exclusions, and independent replication across operators or sites. Practical evaluation should include supervision burden, full workflow time and safe handover when autonomy cannot continue. Finite trials establish demonstrated breadth within tested boundaries; they cannot establish literal universality across patients, complications or procedures.
completion_criteria.label: Stronger: repeated independently replicated performance across anatomy with failures reported

related_concepts.text: ROB-01, Reliable instruction-following physical work in unfamiliar everyday environments, overlaps through perception, planning and adaptation to unfamiliar situations. ROB-02, Autonomous dexterous tool use and in-hand manipulation at human reliability, overlaps through precise instrument control and coordinated manipulation. Whole-procedure surgery adds living anatomy, clinical decisions and irreversible consequences; neither everyday generality nor dexterity alone demonstrates surgical competence.

ROB-06, Untethered intervention at a target inside the living human body, shares the goal of acting therapeutically within a patient. Its defining challenge concerns reaching and intervening at an internal target without a tether. ROB-10 concerns autonomous completion of an entire operation and could use externally supported, tethered instruments. Either capability could be achieved without establishing the other.

ROB-07, Predictive contact mechanics that plans real manipulation, could help a surgical robot anticipate deformation and the consequences of tissue contact. ROB-09, Lifelong on-robot learning that retains and composes physical skills, could help retain and combine operative skills over time. These are potential enabling capabilities: predictive mechanics does not supply clinical judgment, and continual learning does not establish safe whole-procedure performance. Their integration into surgical systems would require its own evaluation.

ROB-03, An artificial muscle that can serve as the main actuator of a useful robot, concerns actuation technology. It could contribute to instrument design but is not a prerequisite specified by this surgical concept. ROB-04, Closed-loop robotic self-reproduction from feedstock, concerns autonomous manufacturing and reproduction; a surgical robot need not manufacture or reproduce itself to complete an operation.

ROB-05, Load-bearing robotic matter that reforms into working machines, concerns reconfigurable physical machinery, while ROB-08, Robot collectives that build functional structures from bulk material, concerns coordinated construction. Reconfiguration or collective coordination might eventually support surgical designs, but neither entry establishes the anatomical understanding, physiological adaptation or full operative coverage required here. These remain distinct innovations.

change_log.change: Preserved ROB-10 and its title, while defining the target as supervised autonomy across a complete operation on living tissue.
change_log.reason: The review supports the concept’s coherence and distinguishes it from task autonomy, teleoperation and operation without an available surgeon.

change_log.change: Replaced an implied present-day absence claim with a dated account of demonstrated capability and remaining documented gaps.
change_log.reason: The supplied evidence concerns May 2025 work, and the freshness record cannot establish field-wide absence as of November 1, 2026.

change_log.change: Retained the eight-of-eight, 100% reported result and 17-task scope while adding prior manual dissection and approximately 10% anatomical exclusions.
change_log.reason: These details preserve the achievement while making its procedural and anatomical coverage explicit.

change_log.change: Explained autonomous task execution alongside manual clip loading, instrument changes, resumption, scissors replacement and three robot reinitializations.
change_log.reason: The broad autonomy language requires operational qualification, and timing excluded manual servicing.

change_log.change: Acknowledged that the ex vivo work addresses some anatomical variation and performs actual cuts.
change_log.reason: Its limitations do not imply an absence of destructive action or adaptation to unseen tissue.

change_log.change: Qualified the journal citation and attributed author response instead of treating their wording or pig-cadaver description as verified.
change_log.reason: The DOI page has no retained material in the supplied source index; the preprint supports ex vivo porcine gallbladder experimentation.

change_log.change: Recast increased capacity, consistency, access and reduced cost as conditional benefits.
change_log.reason: Whole-procedure feasibility alone does not establish clinical reliability, workflow efficiency or staffing benefits.

change_log.change: Retained verification methods as a possible contribution to safety assurance without claiming an established certification benefit.
change_log.reason: The supplied evidence does not substantiate the original general-proof-system certification assertion.

change_log.change: Expanded completion criteria to include assistance accounting, clinical endpoints, replication and explicit operating boundaries.
change_log.reason: The review distinguishes feasibility from reliability and treats the proposed evaluation choices as proposals rather than consensus standards.

change_log.change: Explained relationships with every other supplied roster entry and preserved the review’s access limitations.
change_log.reason: Related enabling capabilities should remain distinct, and readers need to know that the review assessed retained text without inspecting visual evidence.

unresolved_issues: Whether whole-procedure autonomy on living patients had been demonstrated elsewhere by November 1, 2026 remains unassessed because no freshness search record was supplied.
The journal abstract, July 9, 2025 publication details and attributed author response cannot be independently confirmed from the retained materials; the pig-cadaver attribution remains unverified.
The author-reported experimental results were assessed through the retained preprint text; figures and videos were not inspected in the supplied review.
Performance on excluded anatomical anomalies, other unfamiliar conditions and the full in-vivo operative sequence is not established by the eight-specimen phase demonstration.
Procedure-specific sample sizes, safety thresholds, anatomical coverage, permitted assistance and clinical endpoints remain to be defined and justified.
Clinical capacity, consistency, cost and access benefits require outcome and workflow evidence beyond autonomous completion.
No substantive review recommendation was rejected; unverifiable assertions were qualified and unresolved questions were preserved.
